normalized.governing_thought: Margin fell because of promotions, e-commerce and shrink, not mainly wages; a six-lever plan gets back to ~3.0% by FY2028 within the $25M budget
executive_summary: What happened: Operating margin fell from 3.37% to 1.02% in two years (−$35M at FY2025 sales). Store labor explains just 0.30 pt of the 2.35-pt fall. Promotions (0.70), e-commerce fulfillment (0.84) and shrink (0.50) explain 2.04 pts, 87%.

Why the draft plan falls short: Cutting store hours 8% and freezing e-commerce reaches only ~1.5% margin by FY2028 even if the cut costs nothing, once the 2027 wage rise is absorbed. It also puts fresh quality at risk: stores with the fewest labor hours already run 3.1% shrink against 2.3%.

What we recommend: Fix the margin where it was lost: (1) reprice home delivery as tested; (2) cut the money-losing promotions and win back vendor funding; (3) restore receiving and produce routines to cut shrink; (4) schedule labor to demand rather than cut it across the board; (5) grow private label; (6) exit the nine stores with negative four-wall EBITDA, six of them as their leases expire.

What it delivers: Operating income rises from $15.3M to ~$41.5M in FY2028, about 3.0% of ~$1.40B sales, after absorbing a $6.8M wage rise. One-time cost is ~$18M of the $25M ceiling. The base case is thin (2.96%), so ~$10M of contingency levers are worked in parallel.

What to do first: Four moves in the next six months need ~$1.5M of one-time cost and add ~$7.9M a year: roll out delivery pricing, drop loss-making promotion events, reinstate receiving and rotation checks, and refuse the 3% delivery rate rise. This takes run-rate operating income to ~$23M, above the $20M covenant level.
Decisions today: Approve the plan in place of the 8% hours cut; vote on a fix-or-exit test for the three stores with leases beyond 2027; authorise the $25M envelope and a lender briefing.

normalized.recommendation: Fix the margin where it was lost: (1) reprice home delivery as tested; (2) cut the money-losing promotions and win back vendor funding; (3) restore receiving and produce routines to cut shrink; (4) schedule labor to demand rather than cut it across the board; (5) grow private label; (6) exit the nine stores with negative four-wall EBITDA, six of them as their leases expire. Start with four Wave 1 moves (delivery pricing, drop loss-making promotion events, reinstate receiving and rotation checks, refuse the 3% delivery rate rise). Board to approve the plan in place of the 8% hours cut and the FY2028 target of at least 3.0%; vote on the fix-or-exit rule for the three stores with leases beyond 2027 (up to $7.5M); authorise the up-to-$25M one-time envelope; endorse delivery repricing and an early lender briefing.

alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected. Reaches only ~1.5% margin by FY2028 even if the cut costs nothing (~$12.5M–22.5M, 0.8%–1.5%); addresses about 13% of the problem; risks +0.6–0.7 pt shrink (~$10M), checkout waits, stock-outs and weaker fresh; run-rate below $20M covenant if shrink rises ~$10M; freezing e-commerce locks in the ~$10M loss. Replaced by the recommended plan.
Chosen over the 8% blanket cut: ~$5.1M net labor saving, shrink −0.3 pt (+$4.2M), net effect ~$9.3M vs ~$4.5M for the blanket cut if shrink rises as feared.

alternatives_considered.option: Keep home delivery vs. drop it
alternatives_considered.treatment: Delivery kept, as the owners want, at tested $7.99 / $100 pricing with click-and-collect as default; remaining ~$7.6M a year loss is 'the visible cost of that choice'.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: The base case is thin (2.96%): within ~$0.5M of the target, so there is no slack; ~$10M of contingency levers are worked in parallel.
The wage line assumes the 4% minimum-wage rise flows through the entire store pay scale (conservative); if it touches only half the pay scale, margin is ~3.2%.
Only the 2027 minimum-wage step is modelled; other inflation is assumed to pass through prices.
The ~$10M shrink estimate for an 8% cut applies the FY2023–25 pattern; it is an association, not a measured effect.
Promotion sizing assumes 30% of the margin recovered is given back in lost volume.
Vendor funding assumes the 14-pt promotional margin gap is net of funding (~$113M of FY2025 markdowns); if it is gross, the lever needs re-sizing.
Delivery test results (4 stores, 10 weeks) are assumed to scale chain-wide; lost sales valued at 30% new × 20¢.
E-commerce uses finance's 20¢ contribution per new dollar; sales customers would have made in store are treated as adding no contribution.
Private label pace of ~1 pt a year is achievable (vs 0.75 pt historically).
Chain can reach the Q4 shrink level (2.3%); net 3% labor hours reduction achievable without service loss.
The split between the six and the three stores is assumed pro rata to store count; at least 25% of closed-store sales follow to nearby stores.
Only the $7.5M lease-exit cost is from the pack; other one-time costs are planning allowances to be validated by finance.
The pack has no FY2026 actuals; covenant tested on run-rate after Wave 1; FY2026 may land below $20M.
Delivery contract renews in 2026 and may already be signed at +3%.
The comparable-sales claim (+1.8% vs +0.2%) is treated as a correlation and does not control for store differences.
Wave timing assumes the plan is approved in February 2027 (start of FY2027).

Main risks: ValuMart reacting to fewer promotions; execution across six workstreams; vendor resistance; service/fresh impact of scheduling; delivery customer loss; larger wage rise; fewer sales following closed stores.
